data.title: The Structure and Meaning of Second Baruch
data.abstractNote: This thesis is an analysis of Second Baruch, otherwise known as the Syriac Apocalypse of Baruch. It begins with a literary analysis which refines the traditional division of the book into seven parts by making explicit the structure of each part. Parts II through VI are seen as structured according to the following scheme:  (a) introductory prayer of Baruch; (b) dialogue between Baruch and God; (c) speech usually by Baruch, but in part II by God. The argument is made that the author's own emphases can be discovered by paying special attention to the speeches and prayers of Baruch, and by seeing the dialogues as supporting those speeches and prayers. The structures of parts I and VII do not fit the scheme elucidated above. The first section introduces the central concern of the author: the absence of Zion. This section is analyzed in chapter four of this thesis, which deals with the author's attitude toward Zion and the Temple. Its structure follows that of the intercessory bargaining form as found in various parts of the Old Testament. Section VII consists of Baruch's epistle to the exiles and serves as a summary of the major ideas of Second Baruch. Analysis of this section is used throughout the thesis to confirm the results obtained by the investigation of parts I through VI. Second Baruch was written as a reaction to the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 C.E. Its basic message is that although Jerusalem is gone, the Law remains, and that it is through obedience to that Law that one can attain to the new world. In the author's references to this new world (analyzed in chapter three of this thesis) he uses two sets of language. One set stresses the ontological difference between the two worlds (the present one is corruptible and transitory, the future one is eternal). He does this by using both sapiential reasoning and presentation of God's revelation to Baruch. This thesis sees this viewpoint as the author's alteration of a more traditional eschatology, as is found for example in Isaiah. In this latter eschatology, the new world is heaven and earth transformed in a way which corrects all ills. By using both sets of language, the author of Second Baruch reinforces the hope of the people in the future, but stresses the discontinuity between this world and the future one, thereby relativizing the importance of the destruction of Zion and even of its restoration.

data.title: Myatrūtṯā: труднопереводимое понятие сирийской духовной литературы
data.abstractNote: В сирийской духовно-аскетической (мистической) литературе, расцвет которой приходится на V–VIII вв., существует несколько понятий, фундаментальных для системы особой ноосферы в этой традиции. При переводе на другие языки они представляли (и представляют) проблему, неверное решение которой нередко создает совершенно новую языковую и культурную игру смыслов, чуждую для языка оригинала. К таким словам принадлежит сирийское myatrūṯā, ( ), которое обычно переводят как «добродетель», что создает неверное понимание в большинстве контекстов. Именно так (греческим aρετή) его передали греческие переводчики первого тома мар Исхака Ниневийского (Исаака Сирина). В статье вскрывается сложная семантика этого слова, восходящего к основе ytr со значением «напрягать, становиться больше». За идеей преизбытка и напряжения возникает идея совершенства, постепенно переходящая в «нравственное совершенство». В статье дан этимологический и синтаксический анализ слова и его корня. Кроме того, рассмотрены примеры использования слова myatruta в первых шести трактатах Первого тома мар Исхака. Проделанная работа подводит к осознанию необходимой коррекции в понимании и переводе этого слова, так как в большом числе мест оно имеет смысл «аскетизм» или «практика воздержания».

data.title: En syrisk kilde til den ældste kristne nadverforståelse – en analyse af Addai og Maris Nadverbøn
data.abstractNote: The Anaphora of Addai and Mari (A&M) is an ancient Syriac Eucharistic prayer. This article provides a Danish translation of the prayer and presents indications that A&M contains one of the oldest Eucharistic traditions that we know of. It is argued that A&M presents an understanding of the divine presence in the Eucharist that differs from traditional Western and Hellenistic views, and that A&M seems to be influenced by Jewish prayer forms. The article utilises A&M to discuss and broaden commonly held theories about the earliest understanding and development of the Eucharistic ritual.
